[[:db/retract 17592186382208 :answer-field/choices 17592186382209] [:db/retract 17592186382208 :answer-field/choices 17592186382210] [:db/retract 17592186382208 :answer-field/choices 17592186382211] [:db/retract 17592186382208 :answer-field/choices 17592186382212] [:db/retract 17592186382208 :answer-field/choices 17592186382213] [:db/retract 17592186409555 :answer-field/choices 17592186409552] [:db/retract 17592186409555 :answer-field/choices 17592186409539] [:db/retract 17592186409555 :answer-field/choices 17592186409540] [:db/retract 17592186409555 :answer-field/choices 17592186409545] [:db/retract 17592186409555 :answer-field/choices 17592186409547] {:db/id 17592186382207 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}=\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is defined only when $xy>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}=\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is the same

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{z}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186382208 :answer-field/correct "answer-629c6583-5abe-5cd2-8098-b6cded7ee4e3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a318ea21-95fd-5a51-9e1e-c2501bcf0d2e" "answer-395e6ad4-f871-5195-aed0-c82a5612a79c" "answer-629c6583-5abe-5cd2-8098-b6cded7ee4e3" "answer-32e88f5b-98b5-56cf-80ff-82851c3303b7" "answer-410d16c0-a17f-5bb6-8557-36dd6a7c08d7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a318ea21-95fd-5a51-9e1e-c2501bcf0d2e" :answer/id #uuid "a318ea21-95fd-5a51-9e1e-c2501bcf0d2e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy=0,z\ne 0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-395e6ad4-f871-5195-aed0-c82a5612a79c" :answer/id #uuid "395e6ad4-f871-5195-aed0-c82a5612a79c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z>0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-629c6583-5abe-5cd2-8098-b6cded7ee4e3" :answer/id #uuid "629c6583-5abe-5cd2-8098-b6cded7ee4e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32e88f5b-98b5-56cf-80ff-82851c3303b7" :answer/id #uuid "32e88f5b-98b5-56cf-80ff-82851c3303b7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-410d16c0-a17f-5bb6-8557-36dd6a7c08d7" :answer/id #uuid "410d16c0-a17f-5bb6-8557-36dd6a7c08d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ne 0,z<0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186382221 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}?$ 

I. ${f}_{y}(1,1,1)$ is defined

II. ${f}_{z}(0,1,2)$ is defined

III. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,1,1)$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186409559 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186409555 :answer-field/correct "answer-603bfd17-5e73-595d-9e4e-67eb66547b83" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b33e9175-1fe3-525c-84d8-993f2fb37971" "answer-6e5cf9f7-9ed5-55ea-b3dd-342a00251b3b" "answer-1625c29f-0f6c-51a9-9abf-da854c690be8" "answer-603bfd17-5e73-595d-9e4e-67eb66547b83" "answer-d2f2980b-11d7-556d-9928-b285bb77ebda"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b33e9175-1fe3-525c-84d8-993f2fb37971" :answer/id #uuid "b33e9175-1fe3-525c-84d8-993f2fb37971" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6e5cf9f7-9ed5-55ea-b3dd-342a00251b3b" :answer/id #uuid "6e5cf9f7-9ed5-55ea-b3dd-342a00251b3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1625c29f-0f6c-51a9-9abf-da854c690be8" :answer/id #uuid "1625c29f-0f6c-51a9-9abf-da854c690be8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0,\,x+y+z\ne 0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-603bfd17-5e73-595d-9e4e-67eb66547b83" :answer/id #uuid "603bfd17-5e73-595d-9e4e-67eb66547b83" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2f2980b-11d7-556d-9928-b285bb77ebda" :answer/id #uuid "d2f2980b-11d7-556d-9928-b285bb77ebda" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186268907 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}?$

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(4,2)$

$(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{x}{xy} \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186436747 :question/id #uuid "5c311fab-0276-5890-a0ca-a5fc54209d6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-132642"} {:db/id 17592186436748 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}?$

- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(4,2)$
- ${f}_{x}(0,2)$ is defined
- ${f}_{y}(0,2)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(4,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(4,2)=\frac{\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,2) & =\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{16} \\ {f}_{y}(4,2) & =-\frac{2\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{3}}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,2)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,2)=\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\frac{\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{2}}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,2)=-\frac{2\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{3}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186268914 :question/id #uuid "a68d3690-fbcf-53d1-acbf-a5134efed5cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132728" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124466 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9d090462-a031-5f96-ac13-90dac882edab" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "313ed8a6-5624-51e9-8247-921676b60bf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186266577} {:answer/id #uuid "409a59c0-29a1-5253-ba63-e612221ceedc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186266729} {:answer/id #uuid "635f6241-0e3a-5ddf-84d9-85447f3da39e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186267018} {:answer/id #uuid "d3e2402e-0272-58c9-af19-86fc33ef5471" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186268033} {:answer/id #uuid "e54c682f-12fe-57b4-a4b2-763baf12853b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186268168}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "409a59c0-29a1-5253-ba63-e612221ceedc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186266729} :answer-field/id #uuid "61fa50ca-fd4a-5d40-a9dd-ff3a34de4409" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186268584}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,2)$

II. ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

I. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$is defined

II. ${f}_{y}(1,0)$ is defined

III. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+x{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=0\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0/1}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot {e}^{0/1}+0\cdot {e}^{0/1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into ${f}_{y}$, we get

$$
{f}_{y}(1,0)=1\cdot {e}^{1/0}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{0}\cdot {e}^{1/0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1)=1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}+1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=2e \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{1}\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e-e=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186339045 :question/id #uuid "ada5bc24-8a74-58e6-b57b-4b21dfa8df4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-72022" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3ac27dea-917c-5759-bc7e-a294df2c3496" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186336584} {:answer/id #uuid "4dbecb09-2562-5367-8c90-ff2bde5c8c58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186336753} {:answer/id #uuid "52c1132d-973b-57b7-aa9e-9d4fd340d6ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186336793} {:answer/id #uuid "7c32390c-300a-507d-83ee-7cae21fe4401" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186337154} {:answer/id #uuid "e373744d-6349-5033-8db7-c0eba5117ac7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186338016}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336753} :answer-field/id #uuid "a2e66753-277a-5e85-925f-63997e65e3d8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338578}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy(z-1))?$

$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}?$ 

- ${f}_{y}(1,1,1)$ is defined
- ${f}_{z}(0,1,2)$ is defined
- The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(0,1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+y-z}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x+y-z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1,1)=\sqrt{2\cdot 1+1-1}=\sqrt{2},
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot 1+1-1}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(0,1,2)=\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-2}=\sqrt{-1},
$$

which is undefined since the number under the radical is negative.

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1,1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 0+1-1}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only'."} {:db/id 17592186409557 :question/id #uuid "0a3b6388-98bd-5083-8d1c-f60a05890b23" :question/math-academy-id "q-132726" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4257b911-5988-5866-b9ff-6170b641f678" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186409543} {:answer/id #uuid "673d57e2-c509-53cd-86d7-a568bf1e97f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186409546} {:answer/id #uuid "8e6aa6de-7d86-5660-b9a6-8496a3ca7253" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186409548} {:answer/id #uuid "c44c870f-1d5b-5d9f-93d5-da63006f4e75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186409550} {:answer/id #uuid "d4667459-8749-5c76-8a2a-d3b084c75e44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186409551}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409551} :answer-field/id #uuid "e7c2354d-85e6-577f-a722-6c718f129147" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409556}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} {:db/id 17592186409558 :question/id #uuid "538fdcf0-8dcd-525c-becd-0317742dbf1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-72010" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2dbd6ccf-ed91-536c-bc41-cccc05325c4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186409541} {:answer/id #uuid "2ff6ca25-dc52-5f06-b4e5-fccf5f8c424e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186409542} {:answer/id #uuid "5c5e8d7a-13cb-5c4a-af4c-8873999183d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186409544} {:answer/id #uuid "98963520-6ef4-5229-b4a2-12278d12f050" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186409549} {:answer/id #uuid "feeb48aa-dc46-5157-aa75-f72619f1adb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186409553}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409541} :answer-field/id #uuid "90260639-fefe-562c-8509-7dc58803f6c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409554}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}?$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $-1\le xyz\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}}$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(xyz)^{2} & >0 \\ (xyz)^{2} & <1 \\ |xyz| & <1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186125193 :question/id #uuid "0790aa49-4020-5e37-b9fd-2a18a4aa638d" :question/math-academy-id "q-65252"} {:db/id 17592186268902 :question/id #uuid "a66c3ca8-3dc1-5636-a0ae-fd45747b8bcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-132649"} {:db/id 17592186268903 :question/id #uuid "f03ff15b-864a-54f0-95c4-85eaad4622ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-132650"} {:db/id 17592186268904 :question/id #uuid "9c09835a-efb6-5fd7-a6fa-37a21ebe5b95" :question/math-academy-id "q-132651"} {:db/id 17592186339043 :question/id #uuid "329fb25a-c39e-587a-8c51-720f867dc9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72005" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b4579a6-884f-5620-9c48-03f859207fbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}" :db/id 17592186337292} {:answer/id #uuid "aa211335-2ec0-5533-aaf0-0747d0111e9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186337566} {:answer/id #uuid "ab12ccaa-59a3-5391-8885-0e57cfa9220d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<0}" :db/id 17592186337575} {:answer/id #uuid "d30b5af1-be96-52a2-983e-53d94d787930" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186337875} {:answer/id #uuid "d932ef34-432a-58eb-96dc-98456b7b3465" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0}" :db/id 17592186337921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337292} :answer-field/id #uuid "167ce942-9903-5739-b46e-634adbd1db2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338315}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ and

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{z}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}=\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is defined only when $xy>0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}=\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2z\sqrt{xy}}$ is the same

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{z}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{{z}^{2}}$ is defined only when $xy\ge 0$ and $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy\ge 0,z\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xy>0,z\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186409559 :question/id #uuid "5744243e-c58b-5537-916f-bee0cb473253" :question/math-academy-id "q-132654" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124557 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2d7d4db-e9e1-54a0-aadb-42447771855d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "094c985d-13f5-5f69-aeaa-14eacd51632b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}" :db/id 17592186409539} {:answer/id #uuid "1b8221d1-3113-502e-8743-5e1721ad92fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0}" :db/id 17592186409540} {:answer/id #uuid "65397964-92f2-5396-b4dd-4062f6c76e9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186409545} {:answer/id #uuid "83b42671-0c9a-50d8-9e14-5be3dd21c197" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186409547} {:answer/id #uuid "fe8bb828-cf39-59be-bb0e-11477fd6ff9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0,\,x+y+z\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186409552}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "094c985d-13f5-5f69-aeaa-14eacd51632b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}" :db/id 17592186409539} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3c16b06-37a6-5eac-b3ba-318617c8302e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186409555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426720 :question/id #uuid "13585dd1-9ab5-5887-870c-2d899c40d4a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-132652" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a414987-4111-5550-9b84-35b48e518248" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426709} {:answer/id #uuid "c4574d37-c2e2-5922-8956-3143f5bef26f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426712} {:answer/id #uuid "c67ec9fa-9f76-59b9-b6ed-a85557705824" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y>0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426713} {:answer/id #uuid "ee7e5c9b-05ac-5232-9af8-bc55f1d66335" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426715} {:answer/id #uuid "f480f4b0-b440-57d3-be41-894b18986911" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z" :db/id 17592186426716}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426716} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d0f4a07-8c58-5c53-b0aa-71dedf0ab601" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426719}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$

partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

For example, let's consider the function $f(x,y) = \ln(xy).$ We wish to determine the set of values $(x,y)$ on which the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists.

First, we need to find the domain of $f$ since we cannot differentiate $f$ at any point that lies outside of its domain. The natural logarithm is defined only for positive inputs, so the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{ (x,y)\, : \, xy > 0 \}.
$$

Next, we compute the partial derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ (also denoted $f_x$) is not defined at $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is

$$
D_{f_x} = \{ (x,y)\, : \, x \ne 0 \}.
$$

To compute the set where  $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_x})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, xy \gt 0 \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5862db65-6f2d-5256-968d-cb971dd6b2f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2532 17592186125314}} {:db/id 17592186125314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not Imply Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "f23e88d8-c204-5795-b172-b05000a202c3" :step/math-academy-id 11432} {:db/id 17592186125463 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124557 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124366 :question/id #uuid "97192aac-6c1a-5ead-962b-0bf7ab573661" :question/math-academy-id "e-6109"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e2d7d4db-e9e1-54a0-aadb-42447771855d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125001} {:db/id 17592186125193} {:db/id 17592186268902} {:db/id 17592186268903} {:db/id 17592186268904} {:db/id 17592186339043} {:db/id 17592186339044} {:db/id 17592186339046} {:db/id 17592186339047} {:db/id 17592186381048} {:db/id 17592186382207} {:db/id 17592186409559} {:db/id 17592186426720} {:db/id 17592186436749} {:db/id 17592186436751}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist"} :step/id #uuid "c86dfe84-cedf-55cf-bf44-efb12a49ac66" :step/math-academy-id 22675 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125313}}] :activity/title "Partial Differentiability of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124725} {:db/id 17592186125311 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125741 :tutorial/content "The partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

{:db/id 17592186125314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." :tutorial/id #uuid "ca47070b-a1d3-53ad-8f57-2dbd4e770dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2533 :tutorial/title "Partial Differentiability Does Not Imply Continuity"} :step/id #uuid "f23e88d8-c204-5795-b172-b05000a202c3" :step/math-academy-id 11432} {:db/id 17592186125742 :tutorial/content "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,-1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}}\cdot \frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{2\sqrt{xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(1)(-1)}}=-{e}^{\sqrt{-1}}
$$

which is undefined since we have a negative number under the radical.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(-1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(-1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{1}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =\frac{(-1){e}^{\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1}}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot \frac{{e}^{\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}}{2\sqrt{0\cdot 1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II  only'."} :step/id #uuid "06a4b700-aa67-595f-ad77-c3a9c2d08fa3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409563}} {:db/id 17592186409561 :step/content {:db/id 17592186339043 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b4579a6-884f-5620-9c48-03f859207fbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}" :db/id 17592186337292} {:answer/id #uuid "aa211335-2ec0-5533-aaf0-0747d0111e9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186337566} {:answer/id #uuid "ab12ccaa-59a3-5391-8885-0e57cfa9220d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<0}" :db/id 17592186337575} {:answer/id #uuid "d30b5af1-be96-52a2-983e-53d94d787930" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186337875} {:answer/id #uuid "d932ef34-432a-58eb-96dc-98456b7b3465" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0}" :db/id 17592186337921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337292} :answer-field/id #uuid "167ce942-9903-5739-b46e-634adbd1db2c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338315}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "329fb25a-c39e-587a-8c51-720f867dc9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72005" :question/problem "Given that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.
$$

- The function ${g}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is defined only when ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}>0}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1786d23c-6b2b-5b25-8a34-a3df54af58bf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409560}} {:db/id 17592186409562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186335822 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d023b1a-e54c-5a09-986e-c64e8ea0ce13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186333981} {:answer/id #uuid "b6aad436-bdd3-559d-8993-f9ec2e12126f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186334588} {:answer/id #uuid "c0e883eb-0fef-5f4c-9a6c-403643063014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186334661} {:answer/id #uuid "d284e0b7-af0b-5d1a-99e5-eded90f88db0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186334828} {:answer/id #uuid "f6908825-368b-5836-af84-e8c9e08903f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186335153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186334828} :answer-field/id #uuid "c726d8d6-8230-5663-b6a4-988732e72c43" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335603}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b22bd39f-49d5-56c7-8797-705e83876e55" :question/math-academy-id "q-65255" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=xy{e}^{x/y}?$

I. ${f}_{x}(0,1)$is defined

II. ${f}_{y}(1,0)$ is defined

III. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+x{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=0\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0/1}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot {e}^{0/1}+0\cdot {e}^{0/1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into ${f}_{y}$, we get

$$
{f}_{y}(1,0)=1\cdot {e}^{1/0}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{0}\cdot {e}^{1/0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1)=1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}+1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=2e \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{1}\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e-e=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} :step/id #uuid "488b6ab6-cae5-5979-9b52-c3723c3f093b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186409561}} {:db/id 17592186409563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186409559 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "094c985d-13f5-5f69-aeaa-14eacd51632b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}" :db/id 17592186409539} {:answer/id #uuid "1b8221d1-3113-502e-8743-5e1721ad92fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x+y+z>0}" :db/id 17592186409540} {:answer/id #uuid "65397964-92f2-5396-b4dd-4062f6c76e9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0,\,y\ne 0,\,z\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186409545} {:answer/id #uuid "83b42671-0c9a-50d8-9e14-5be3dd21c197" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0}" :db/id 17592186409547} {:answer/id #uuid "fe8bb828-cf39-59be-bb0e-11477fd6ff9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0,\,x+y+z\ne 0}" :db/id 17592186409552}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186409539} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3c16b06-37a6-5eac-b3ba-318617c8302e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186409555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5744243e-c58b-5537-916f-bee0cb473253" :question/math-academy-id "q-132654" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $xyz>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,x\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0}.\end{aligned}

- ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$

$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

$$

$$

$$

$f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})?$

- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
- ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
- ${f}_{y}(0,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+1}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot (-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have 

$$
f(\sqrt{3},1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\sqrt{3},1) & =\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}_{y}(\sqrt{3},1) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,\sqrt{3})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{0}{1})=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,1)=-\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."} :step/id #uuid "be87cbb6-8a21-5895-a193-08d9d1a311c5"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4257b911-5988-5866-b9ff-6170b641f678" :question/math-academy-id "q-72022" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy(z-1))?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(1,1,2)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{x}(1,2,3)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot y(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot x(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{z-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.  

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(3,2,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2\cdot (1-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined.

- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot (2-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,2) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2,3) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III  only'."} :step/id #uuid "30fe1f41-c7f8-5010-a260-ed3ef63a4abc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426726}} {:db/id 17592186426723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186268914 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "313ed8a6-5624-51e9-8247-921676b60bf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186266577} {:answer/id #uuid "409a59c0-29a1-5253-ba63-e612221ceedc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186266729} {:answer/id #uuid "635f6241-0e3a-5ddf-84d9-85447f3da39e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186267018} {:answer/id #uuid "d3e2402e-0272-58c9-af19-86fc33ef5471" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186268033} {:answer/id #uuid "e54c682f-12fe-57b4-a4b2-763baf12853b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186268168}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186266729} :answer-field/id #uuid "61fa50ca-fd4a-5d40-a9dd-ff3a34de4409" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268584}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a68d3690-fbcf-53d1-acbf-a5134efed5cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-132728" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$

II. ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} :step/id #uuid "574ad7f2-698f-50d6-8eee-36f6145d16e5"} {:db/id 17592186426724 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125001 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "323e1e26-806d-5103-9c5b-05be999f86f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}" :db/id 17592186426704} {:answer/id #uuid "3f71ffa0-c375-5e54-a4b4-82c47e1862fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0<xyz<1\}" :db/id 17592186426705} {:answer/id #uuid "58a495bb-1535-5c0c-8153-9cddc1a1d72c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186426707} {:answer/id #uuid "66b51739-6d9c-59ee-81d0-4f21e588a03b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}" :db/id 17592186426708} {:answer/id #uuid "ab77e5e6-52f4-5889-9394-0781e3a0ecd5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y,z)\,:\,xyz>0\}" :db/id 17592186426711}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426704} :answer-field/id #uuid "6476017e-359c-522d-8dec-b6d7cd0832c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122606}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f23029a5-0003-5b31-a62a-a58e0c29de2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-36527" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $-1\le xyz\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}}$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(xyz)^{2} & >0 \\ (xyz)^{2} & <1 \\ |xyz| & <1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d1a2f4bc-c2ad-5ea9-bbc9-a5f92a8d1b61" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426725}} {:db/id 17592186426725 :step/content {:db/id 17592186426721 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26545a18-833f-5099-8272-edbb2a66edaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}" :db/id 17592186426703} {:answer/id #uuid "4d5bdc4f-f2f7-5295-b2ba-aa4588793c88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy\ge 0\}" :db/id 17592186426706} {:answer/id #uuid "a9d10897-b8cf-5fad-b81e-91fbcac64c00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "${f}_{y}$ exists everywhere on the $xy$-plane" :db/id 17592186426710} {:answer/id #uuid "ebb0a6cd-e867-5b85-88ef-cd845e6904a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy<0\}" :db/id 17592186426714} {:answer/id #uuid "ff439fa7-e5eb-53d6-8dc0-e5396941eb06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}" :db/id 17592186426717}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426717} :answer-field/id #uuid "4cca11fe-f3bb-53ee-b7b6-de2725b37ad7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426718}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "abe73768-66b7-589e-98db-9176084649e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-72006" :question/problem "Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{x}{xy} \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$

$$

$$

$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$

$$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "d1a2f4bc-c2ad-5ea9-bbc9-a5f92a8d1b61" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426725}} {:db/id 17592186426722 :step/content {:db/id 17592186339045 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3ac27dea-917c-5759-bc7e-a294df2c3496" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186336584} {:answer/id #uuid "4dbecb09-2562-5367-8c90-ff2bde5c8c58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186336753} {:answer/id #uuid "52c1132d-973b-57b7-aa9e-9d4fd340d6ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186336793} {:answer/id #uuid "7c32390c-300a-507d-83ee-7cae21fe4401" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186337154} {:answer/id #uuid "e373744d-6349-5033-8db7-c0eba5117ac7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186338016}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336753} :answer-field/id #uuid "a2e66753-277a-5e85-925f-63997e65e3d8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338578}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ada5bc24-8a74-58e6-b57b-4b21dfa8df4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-72022" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy(z-1))?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(1,1,2)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{x}(1,2,3)$ is defined" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$

$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.  

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(3,2,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2\cdot (1-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined.

- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot (2-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,2) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2,3) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III  only'."} :step/id #uuid "30fe1f41-c7f8-5010-a260-ed3ef63a4abc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426726}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$

$$

exists." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{x}{xy} \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d34189a3-bcaf-5744-9e6b-ec97ad8307d1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186426722}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26545a18-833f-5099-8272-edbb2a66edaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
The course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1013 "MML" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1014 #uuid "1ee987ec-c9ff-5d2f-91f4-4de8079c0eac" 17592186045417] 17592186046982 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating 17592186124557 17592186045417] [17592186125741 1064 "The partial derivative of a function exists where the original function is defined *and* the partial derivative is defined.

For example, let's consider the function $f(x,y) = \ln(xy).$ We wish to determine the set of values $(x,y)$ on which the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists.

First, we need to find the domain of $f$ since we cannot differentiate $f$ at any point that lies outside of its domain. The natural logarithm is defined only for positive inputs, so the domain of $f$ is 

$$
D_f = \{ (x,y)\, : \, xy > 0 \}.
$$

Next, we compute the partial derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ (also denoted $f_x$) is not defined at $x=0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is

$$
D_{f_x} = \{ (x,y)\, : \, x \ne 0 \}.
$$

To compute the set where  $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists, we take the intersection of the domain of the original function $(D_f)$ with the domain of the partial derivative $(D_{f_x})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,x\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists on the set $\{ (x,y)\, : \, xy \gt 0 \}.$" 17592186045417] [17592186125741 1065 2532 17592186045417] [17592186125741 1066 #uuid "5862db65-6f2d-5256-968d-cb971dd6b2f1" 17592186045417] [17592186125741 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186125742 1064 "From single-variable calculus, if a function $y=f(x)$ is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point.

But for a multivariable function, even if all partial derivatives are defined at a certain point, it **does not mean** that the function is continuous at that point!

The reason why partial differentiability does not imply continuity in the case of a multivariable function is that

- the existence of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ depend only on the behavior of $f$ parallel to the $x$- and $y$-axes, whereas

- the continuity of $f$ depends on its behavior as we approach $(x_0,y_0)$ from any direction.

For example, let's consider the following multivariable function:

![](images/cb/cb5aad599789d1e317ff3ddc07eaa418e80469307f67e98e2108660fc7d15701.svg)

The function $f$ is defined at the point $(0,0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f(0,0)=0
$$

Likewise, the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ are both defined at the point $(0,0).$ We can compute them using the limit definition of the partial derivative, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0+h,0)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(h)(0)}{{h}^{2}+{0}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,0) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[f(0,0+h)-f(0,0)] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[\frac{(0)(h)}{{0}^{2}+{h}^{2}}-0] \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}[0-0] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So the partial derivatives both exist at $(0,0).$ We will now show that the function is not continuous at $(0,0).$

For the function $f$ to be continuous at $(0,0),$ the limit of the function must be equal to the function value, regardless of the path taken. So, we must have

$$
\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to (0,0)}  f(x,y) = f(0,0) =0.
$$

However, this is not the case here. When we evaluate the limit along the path $y=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y)\to (0,0)\,\,y=x}f(x,y) & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{x\cdot x}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function $f(x,y)$ is *not* continuous at the point $(0,0),$ even though both of its partial derivatives exist there." 17592186045417] [17592186125742 1065 2533 17592186045417]
